pages.x: By the first century BC Rome ruled the Mediterranean, but its Republic, run by elected magistrates and the Senate, was breaking down. Soldiers were loyal to the generals who paid them, and Sulla had already marched on Rome itself. Caesar, Pompey and Crassus made a private pact to share power.

In January 49 BC the Senate ordered Caesar, fresh from conquering Gaul, to give up his army. Instead he led a legion across the Rubicon, the stream at the edge of his province, which made him an enemy of the state. The die is cast, he is said to have quoted.

Pompey and much of the Senate fled to Greece. At Pharsalus in 48 BC Caesar's veterans beat Pompey's larger army. Pompey escaped to Egypt, where the advisers of the boy king Ptolemy XIII had him stabbed as he stepped ashore, hoping to please Caesar.

pages.t: A queen in a bedding sack
pages.x: In Alexandria, the young queen Cleopatra, driven out by her brother, had herself carried in to Caesar hidden in a sack for bedding, Plutarch says. Caesar took her side, won a short war in the streets of Alexandria and made her ruler of Egypt.

Caesar came home master of Rome. He pardoned many enemies and gave Rome a new calendar of 365 days with a leap year, which, slightly mended, is the one we use. Early in 44 BC he was made dictator for life. To many senators that made him a king in all but name.

On 15 March 44 BC a group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed Caesar 23 times at a meeting of the Senate in a hall by Pompey's theatre. They cried that Rome was free again. It was not: within months there was civil war again.

Caesar's heir, his 18-year-old great-nephew Octavian, joined Mark Antony to destroy the assassins at Philippi in 42 BC. Then the two fell out. Antony allied with Cleopatra, and at Actium in 31 BC Octavian's admiral Agrippa beat their fleet. A year later both took their own lives in Egypt.

In 27 BC the Senate gave Octavian a new name, Augustus. He never called himself king, and claimed he had restored the Republic, keeping its Senate and consuls. But he commanded the armies and decided everything, and those who ruled after him were emperors.

The Republic's fall brought the Roman world two centuries of peace under emperors, but it ended Rome's long experiment with elected government. Its story, of a free state lost to ambition, haunted the founders of later republics, who borrowed its Senate and its words.
